project.name: How does «My Library» work?
project.title: My Library, explained in depth
project.oneLiner: A web app for borrowing books from a neighborhood library. Readers search for a book and reserve it, get an email two days before it's due, and the librarian adds books from a private dashboard. This is a fictional sample that shows what the page looks like.

analogy.title: Meet the library staff
analogy.intro: A real library has a reader, the shelves, a front desk, a librarian, a loan ledger and a postman. The app has the same jobs.

cast.job: You search for a book and press «Reserve».
Show the books and the search results. They never reserve anything themselves; they pass your request on.
Checks that you're a member before letting your request through.
The only one allowed to lend books. Checks a copy is free, records the loan and sets the due date.
Keeps every book, who borrowed it and when it's due back.
Comes by every morning and reminds anyone whose book is due soon.
cast.handoff: “Reminder: return your book in two days”

analogy.bigIdea: Each part has one job: the screen shows, the front desk checks, the librarian decides, the ledger keeps, and the postman reminds.

flow.title: What happens when you reserve a book?
flow.intro: Follow one press of «Reserve» until the loan is saved and the due date appears.

steps.title: You press «Reserve»
steps.text: The screen calls `reserve()` with the book's id.

steps.title: The request leaves for the server
steps.text: The sign-in token is added and `POST /loans` goes out.

steps.title: The front desk checks you
steps.text: If the token is valid, the reader is known and the request goes through.

steps.title: The librarian decides
steps.text: Counts the copies on loan. If one is left, records the loan and sets the due date.

steps.title: Saved
steps.text: A new row with the due date lands in the `loans` table.

steps.title: The screen updates
steps.text: Your loans are loaded again and «Reserved, return it by …» appears.

moreFlows.title: How do you sign in without a password?
moreFlows.intro: One link in your inbox is enough.

steps.title: You type your email
steps.text: The screen sends the address to the server.

steps.title: A short-lived token
steps.text: A token valid for 15 minutes is created and stored.

steps.title: The link arrives
steps.text: An email with a link that carries the token.

steps.title: You click the link
steps.text: The server swaps the short-lived token for a sign-in token kept in the browser.

moreFlows.title: Who sends the return reminder?
moreFlows.intro: Nobody presses a button here: the server runs the job on its own every morning.

steps.title: 8 in the morning
steps.text: The timer the server set up at startup calls the job.

steps.title: Find loans due soon
steps.text: Loads every open loan due in two days.

steps.title: Send the reminder
steps.text: One email per reader with the book and its due date.

Each loan belongs to one reader.

events.title: First commit
events.text: A search page and a fixed list of books in a JSON file.

events.title: Reservations
events.text: `loanService` appears. This is where the “a free copy or no loan” rule began.

events.title: Moving to PostgreSQL
events.text: Prisma replaced the JSON file. That's why there's a `prisma/` folder.

events.title: Email sign-in
events.text: Passwords were removed. That's why there's a `login_tokens` table.

events.title: Return reminders
events.text: The daily job was added, with its own due-date math separate from `loanService`.

items.title: Two loans for the last copy at the same moment
items.text: `createLoan()` counts the copies and then adds the loan in two separate steps. If two readers reserve the last copy together, both can succeed.

items.title: Adding books doesn't check for the librarian
items.text: The front end hides the dashboard from readers, but the server's `POST /books` route accepts any signed-in reader.

items.title: No waitlist
items.text: When every copy is out, the reader only sees «Not available» and can't ask to be told when one comes back.

items.title: The due date is worked out in two places
items.text: `dueDate()` and `dueInTwoDays()` each compute the loan length their own way. Changing `LOAN_DAYS` alone doesn't move the reminder.

items.title: Search reads the whole table
items.text: Search uses `contains` with no index on the title, so it slows down as the library grows.

glossary.meaning: A reusable piece of the interface, like `BookCard`.
A React function that keeps state or loads data, like `useLoans`.
An address the server answers on, like `POST /loans`.
A step every request passes through before its route, like `requireReader`.
Where the business rules live, like “no loan without a free copy”.
The description of the tables and their columns in `schema.prisma`.
A group of writes that all succeed or all fail.
Code the server runs on its own at a set time, like the morning reminder.
A secret string that tells the server who you are on every request.
A file that changes the database's shape one step at a time.

exercises.title: Change the loan length
exercises.text: Make it 21 days instead of 14, then reserve a book and look at the new due date.

exercises.title: Change the «not available» message
exercises.text: Write something kinder for the reader.
exercises.after: NO_COPY: "Every copy is out right now. Try again in a few days",

exercises.title: Read and explain
exercises.text: Why doesn't `available()` need an “available” column in the books table?
exercises.answer: Because the number of free copies is computed every time: copies minus the loans not yet returned. There's no stored number that someone could forget to update.

exercises.title: Trace the reminder
exercises.text: Change `LOAN_DAYS` to 21. Does the reminder email move? Follow the third flow to find out.
exercises.answer: No. The job computes the date with 14 written inside it. The fix is to call `dueDate()` from `loanService` instead of doing its own math.

figures.title: Where does each part run?
figures.caption: The front end runs in the browser; only the server talks to the database and the email service.
figures.alt: The reader uses a React front end that calls an Express server over HTTPS; the server uses PostgreSQL through Prisma and sends email every morning.
